title: Healthy Tech & AI Boundaries Plan
goal: Your kid helps set their own screen and AI limits, instead of having them handed down. They notice how they use screens, how they feel after, decide what's fair and healthy for them, agree on a plan with you and check it after a few weeks, so the limits feel like theirs.
need: A week of noticing their usual screen time
A timer, or your devices' screen-time settings (Screen Time on Apple, Family Link on Android)

academics.subject: Health
academics.text: how screens affect mood, energy and sleep

academics.subject: Communication
academics.text: making a case and agreeing on a plan

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is setting screen limits for them and enforcing them alone. Your job is to let them notice, ask what they think is fair, decide together, and then let the plan, not you, do the stopping.

plan.what: Notice screen use and how they feel (Steps 1 and 2).
Decide what's fair and agree on the plan (Steps 3 and 4).
Check the plan and adjust it (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They ask for more time every day
troubleshoot.a: Asking is fine. Point to the plan you agreed on together, and save changes for the check-in.

troubleshoot.q: Siblings say it's unfair they get different limits
troubleshoot.a: Fair isn't the same. Talk about what each one uses screens for, and let them hear the reasons.

troubleshoot.q: They want to lower the limit, then struggle
troubleshoot.a: Great sign that they're taking it seriously. Adjust at the check-in, not in the moment.

lesson.text: Limits kids help set are limits they're more likely to respect. When they notice how screens make them feel, say what's fair, and agree on a plan with you, the screen turning off isn't a fight; it's the plan they made.

model.line: Each kid said what would be fair and healthy for them.
Different needs mean different limits, and they heard why.
A different limit for each, agreed together.
The screen shuts off when time's up. They ask for more, but don't fuss at a no.

lesson.modelNote: The limits aren't the same, and they don't have to be. Because the kids helped decide, the 'no' at the end lands as their own plan, not a punishment.

steps.title: Log a screen week
steps.why: Most people guess their screen time wrong. Noticing comes before deciding.
steps.kid: For a week, your kid notes what they use screens for and roughly how long, using the Screen week card in the Healthy Tech Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Track yours too, honestly. Kids notice when grown-ups have different rules for themselves.
ask: What do you use screens for most?
Which screen time felt worth it?
steps.tip: Sort it into watching, playing, making and learning. Not all screen time is the same.

levels.explore: Each day, draw what you did on a screen.
levels.develop: Track a week, sorted into watching, playing, making and learning.
levels.extend: Track a week, then work out what share of your time was making or learning.

steps.title: Notice how you feel after
steps.why: Screens change mood and energy. Seeing it themselves is more convincing than being told.
steps.kid: After screen time, your kid checks in with themselves, using the How do I feel? card: mood, energy, wanting to move or do something.
steps.you: Say what you notice too, kindly: 'You seemed grumpier after the long session yesterday.'
ask: How do you feel right after?
How do you feel after a screen-free day?
steps.tip: Compare a long screen day with a screen-free one. The difference usually speaks for itself.

levels.explore: Point to a face that shows how you feel after screens.
levels.develop: Rate mood and energy after screens for a week.
levels.extend: Find the point in a session where your mood turns, like after 20 minutes or after the second episode.

steps.title: Name what's fair for you
steps.why: Kids are often fairer about their own limits than you'd expect, when they're asked.
steps.kid: Your kid writes what they think would be fair and healthy for them, and why, using the What's fair? card: how long, for what, and when.
steps.you: Listen first. Then share what you think, and why. Different kids can have different needs.
ask: How much screen time feels fair to you?
What do you need screens for, and what's just for fun?
steps.tip: Include AI here too: what it's for in your house, like looking something up together, and what it's not for, like chatting as a friend or doing their writing.

levels.explore: Say how much screen time you think is fair, with a parent.
levels.develop: Write your fair limit, what it's for, and why.
levels.extend: Write your limit, and argue for it with your own data from Steps 1 and 2.

steps.title: Agree on a plan
steps.why: A plan both sides agreed on doesn't need to be enforced every day.
steps.kid: Your family talks it through and fills in Our screen plan at the end of the guide, one for each kid, using the Plan ideas card.
steps.you: Decide together, then let the device or a timer do the stopping, so you don't have to.
ask: When can we talk about changing it?
steps.tip: Automatic limits, like a screen that shuts off, take the fight out of the end.

levels.explore: Help choose your limit, and set the timer with a parent.
levels.develop: Agree on your plan, sign it and set the limits on the device.
levels.extend: Write the plan for a trip or a holiday week, when the usual rules don't fit.

steps.title: Check it and adjust
steps.why: Needs change. A plan you check stays fair.
steps.kid: After a few weeks, your kid looks at how the plan worked, using the Check-in card, and suggests one change if they want.
steps.you: Take their suggestions seriously. Change the plan at the check-in, not in the middle of an argument.
ask: What would you change, and why?
steps.tip: Put the check-in date on the calendar. It gives requests for more time a place to go.

levels.explore: Say one thing you like about the plan, and one you'd change.
levels.develop: Look at a few weeks, and suggest one change with a reason.
levels.extend: Compare how you felt before and after the plan, and present it to the family.

skills.name: Self-control

conclusion.headline: Their screen limits are theirs, not just yours.
conclusion.text: In a few weeks, the end of screen time should feel boring: a timer, a quick 'can I have five more?', a no, and on to something else. Boring is the goal.
conclusion.celebrate: When they stop without a fuss, say: 'You stuck to the plan you helped make. That's real self-control.'
extensions: Swap roles for a day: the kids write a fair limit for a parent, and the parent tries it
Pick a charging spot outside the bedrooms where every device, grown-ups' too, sleeps at night
Compare your Step 1 guesses with the device's own screen-time report, and see who guessed closest
Agree on a family 'phones away' signal for conversations, and use it on grown-ups too

signs: They ask for more time without fussing at a no
They say how screens make them feel
They suggest changes at the check-in, not in the moment
makeItReal: This week, ask each kid what screen limit feels fair to them and why. Then sit down together and write their plan.

fromHome.text: We set each kid's screen limit together: they both said what would be fair and healthy for them, and we made a plan. When the time is up, the screen shuts down. They often ask for more, but they don't fuss when we say no.
